newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar to up oil/condensate capacity to 910,000 b/d.
newsitem.headline: Qatar to up oil/condensate capacity to 910,000 b/d.

text.p: Qatar aims to lift its combined crude and oil condensate output capacity to 910,000 barrels per day (bpd) by 2000, a senior official said on Wednesday.
"The oil fields will contribute 710,000 bpd of crude and the North Field gas around 200,000 bpd of condensates by 2000," the official at the Ministry of Energy and Industry told Reuters.
Qatar, a producer in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), produces over 520,000 bpd of oil and around 75,000 bpd of condensates.
The official admitted that the small Gulf Arab state was producing above its OPEC quota.
"But the oil production will be cut back to bring the six-month average in line with our OPEC quota of 378,000 bpd," said the official, who declined to be named.
"Much of the increase in the capacity will come from new fields which have gone on stream or are about to go on stream," he said.
In the past two years, Qatar has brought two new fields on stream and redeveloped an ageing field under production sharing agreements with foreign firms.
The offshore Al Shaheen field, operated by Danish Maersk Oil, contributes 45,000 bpd and Al Rayyan, operated by the U.S. Atlantic Richfield Company (Arco), contributes 30,000 bpd.

The ageing Idd El Shargi North Dome, where output had dipped to less than 20,000 bpd two years ago, currently produces 80,000 bpd, according to its operator, Occidental Petroleum Corp of the United States.

Officials at the state's Qatar General Petroleum Corp said plans were also under way to further raise the capacity at these fields. Occidental and Maersk are working on schemes to increase the capacity to 150,000 bpd each and Arco to 45,000-50,000 bpd.

Additionally, a new field operated by France's Elf Aquitaine is due to go on stream by the end of the month. The Al Khaleej field, discovered by the French company in 1991, is due to produce 22,000 bpd initially, eventually rising to 35,000-45,000 bpd.
Qatar has also awarded production sharing contracts to the U.S. companies Chevron and Pennzoil for other blocks. But no major discoveries have been reported.
For condensates, which fetch higher prices than crude oil, Qatar pins its hopes on the increased gas production at the North Field -- the world's largest single reservoir of natural gas.

The first phase of the field -- dedicated to domestic industries -- has already given 45,000-50,000 bpd of condensates for two years and one of the three trains (production units) at Qatar Liquefied Gas Company (Qatargas) has begun yielding 25,000-30,000 bpd since September last.
The second train at Qatargas went on stream last week and the third train is to be added later this year, which will together give another 50,000 bpd of condensates.
Production will be increased further by 70,000-75,000 bpd when the state's second LNG project -- the Ras Laffan LNG Company -- goes on stream in July 1999, said the QGPC official.
